nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the familiar prose of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Essayist and letter-writer, a London clerk by profession, who wrote as Elia and became the most admired practitioner of familiar prose between the spectatorial essay and the Victorian essay.
biography: Lamb was born in London into a family long in the service of the Inner Temple, the elder brother of Mary Lamb. He was educated at Christ's Hospital, where Samuel Taylor Coleridge was a schoolfellow and remained a friend for life, and in 1792 he was placed in the East India Company's accounts office at India House, where he worked as a clerk until his retirement in 1825. His early ambition was the stage, and the plays and verses of those years are lost. On 18 March 1796 Mary, in an attack of insanity, killed their mother, and Lamb thenceforward lived with her as her guardian and companion through recurring illness, quarrels and reconciliation. He contributed occasional verse, essays and theatrical criticism to the morning papers from the 1790s, published a selection of the old dramatists with observations in 1808, and worked with his sister on books for children. From 1820 the Elia papers began to appear in periodicals and were collected in 1823 and again in 1833; his letters, much imitated in the century after his death, were published in full only after him. He died at Edmonton in December 1842 of erysipelas and was buried in the churchyard there.
literary_profile: His work is almost wholly prose of a personal kind: the Elia essays and their sequel, a book of old-play specimens with commentary, an editorial and collaborative share in children's books, and a body of letters that he treated as a form of essay. He wrote occasional verse and dramatic criticism, and projected histories and scholarship that he never completed. The characteristic piece is a short meditative essay on a London or a country scene, on the theatre, on books, or on the poor, which wanders from anecdote to reflection and returns to the writer's own life. His subject is memory, friendship, the pleasures of the town, the ruined eighteenth-century house of his childhood, and the tender treatment of the failings of the mind.
stylistic_characteristics: A colloquial yet elaborately allusive prose, full of half-quoted phrases from the old drama and from the Bible, with Latinate inversions, parenthetical self-correction, sudden tenderness under irony, and a persona that admits its own fictions. The sentences imitate the rhythms of talk and of the seventeenth-century writers together; the humour is self-deprecatory and the pathos is never separated from it.
intellectual_concerns: The essayist's persona as a moral and social mask; sympathy with the poor, the servants, the outcast and the insane; the value of the old plays as a school of imagination; the lost haunts and houses of childhood; the claims of duty and dependence within a family; the place of literature in an ordinary working life.
historical_significance: With Hazlitt he defined the Romantic prose essay, and Elia supplied the model of the familiar essayist that the Victorians inherited, most obviously in the essayists of the 1840s and in Stevenson's treatment of the essay voice. His edition and commentary helped establish the modern serious reading of the Jacobean and Caroline dramatists, and his letters form one of the principal records of London literary society between the 1790s and the 1840s.
major_influences: Christ's Hospital and its masters
the friendship and example of Coleridge
the old English dramatists, especially the Jacobean and Caroline city comedy
the spectatorial essay tradition of Addison and Steele
the London theatres, picture galleries and bookshops of his own time
the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer as a stock of phrase
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of Mary Lamb's share in the children's books and in some of the papers printed over his name is debated; the plays and most of the early writings are lost and can only be dated approximately; and the part of the Elia voice that is a self-portrait and the part that is invention cannot be separated.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; children's and educational writing of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Writer of books for children and of educational and religious works for young readers, and the collaborator with her brother in the retelling of Shakespeare that became a standard of nineteenth-century childhood.
biography: Lamb was born in London, the younger sister of Charles Lamb, and was largely self-taught in a household in her brother's keeping. She began to publish for a juvenile market in the early years of the century, contributing a biography of the dramatists to a children's history series and writing verse and prose for the juvenile libraries. With her brother she retold the plays in a volume published in 1807, and she afterwards continued to work for children and to take part in the family's collaborative books. She suffered recurrent attacks of insanity, of which the deadliest was that of 18 March 1796, when she killed her mother; the illness governed the terms of her life and her brother's, and she was in and out of care for the rest of it. She died at Edmonton in May 1847 and was buried there beside her brother.
literary_profile: Her writing is chiefly didactic and for the young: retold fiction, a history of the dramatists written for juvenile readers, and other educational pieces, alongside the share in the collaborative tales and in the joint children's books that were printed over one or both names. The manner of the retellings is plain, brisk and moral, addressed to a child's capacity rather than to a child's fancy, and it carries an unusual weight of quotation from the original plays.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, unornamented narrative prose, close paraphrasing of dramatic speech, an economical moral framing, and a directness of address to the young reader; where her work is joint with her brother's, the plainer narrative manner is the distinguishable element.
intellectual_concerns: The education and moral formation of children; the transmission of Shakespeare to readers too young for the plays; the conduct of a life constrained by illness; dependence, duty and secrecy within a family.
historical_significance: The retellings she made with her brother became the standard introduction to Shakespeare for Victorian childhoods and are still in print, and her case has become central to the modern reassessment of authorship, collaboration and mental illness in Romantic-era writing, which has restored her name to works long printed under one author alone.
major_influences: The plays of Shakespeare and the eighteenth-century editions of them
the juvenile literature and educational publishing of the 1790s and early 1800s
her brother's example and household
the religious and moral writing addressed to young women of the period
biographical_uncertainty: The division of the plays between her and her brother in the volume of 1807 rests on later testimony and is variously reported, several of her works are printed without a name or over a shared title-page, and the intervals and severity of her illness are recorded only in the letters and reminiscences of the family.

birthplace: Bath, Somerset, in a family of Bristol merchants and dissenters
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, prose-writer and historian, of the Lake school and of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Poet of the Eastern and national epic, historian and biographer, and the most prolific and most various of the three Lake writers of the first generation, whose long career carried him from the radicalism of the 1790s to the laureateship and the establishment letters of the 1820s and 1830s.
biography: Southey was born at Bath into a Bristol family, was educated largely at Bristol grammar school and entered Balliol College, Oxford in 1792, where he made the acquaintance that led to the American communitarian scheme; he was intended for the church but abandoned the design of orders, and after a short stay in Scotland and an attempt at the law he lived by his pen. He married in 1795 the elder of the two sisters whose sister his friend of the scheme had first married, and after years in the west he settled in 1802 at Greta Hall in Keswick, where the lake country gave the group its name. The epics of the first decade, with the Welsh romance and the Hindu tale, made him the most conspicuous narrative poet of the day, and his later work was chiefly historical and biographical: a history of Brazil, a history of the Peninsular war, lives of the admiral of Trafalgar and of the founder of Methodism, a miscellaneous prose series and a vast correspondence. He accepted the laureateship in 1813 along with a government recognition of his studies, married a second time in 1829 to a writer of the north, and in March 1843 a fire at Greta Hall destroyed part of his library and hastened his death.
literary_profile: His poetry runs from the republican epic of the Maid of Orleans through the Eastern tales and the Welsh legend of the discoverer to the later romance and the national and religious verse of the laureate years; his prose includes biography, history, letters of travel, controversy and miscellany. The ambition of a national epic and of a national history governed his life, and he was the busy centre of the literary and publishing business of the Lakes. His present reputation rests on the prose life of the admiral, on the letters, and on the record of the radical writings of his youth.
stylistic_characteristics: In verse a fluent and stately blank verse and a deliberate experiment in an accentual and reiterated stanza, with narrative plainness and a wealth of descriptive matter; in prose a clear, brisk and often witty style of narrative and argument, direct in the letters and comprehensive in the historical and biographical books.
intellectual_concerns: The epic, the national poem and the machinery of the Eastern religions; Providence, law and obedience in the moral government of the world; the history, character and settlement of nations; the condition of the church and of letters as a profession; the duties of the writer to the state and to the public.
historical_significance: As the prolific narrative poet of the 1800s he made the Eastern and national romance in verse a leading form of the day, and as historian, biographer, letter-writer and editor he was an institutional centre of Romantic letters; his life of the admiral became the standard English biography of the national hero. His early radical writings and his later establishment were used by rivals to define the politics of the Lake school, and the long review controversy over his epic career is a permanent chapter of Romantic literary history.
major_influences: The romantic and Eastern tales in verse and the prose romances of the East then coming into translation
the older English epics and the Miltonic blank verse
the ballad and minstrely revival of the 1790s
the historians and the travellers of the Peninsula
the friendship and partnership of the poet of Christ's Hospital and of the bard of the Lakes

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, critic and thinker of the Romantic period, of the Lake school and of the Unitarian and German-influenced tradition of ideas
literary_identity: Poet of the supernatural ballad and of the visionary fragment, founder-critic of the Romantic theory of imagination, and moral and religious writer whose prose affected nineteenth-century thought more widely than that of any contemporary except one essayist.
biography: Coleridge was the youngest but one of the ten children of a Devonshire clergyman who kept a grammar school, and after his father's death he was placed at Christ's Hospital in London, where one of his schoolfellows became the essayist of the familiar style. At Jesus College, Cambridge he formed the acquaintance that led to the communitarian scheme for a settlement on the American frontier, and in 1795, having left the university without a degree, he married one of the Fricker sisters, whose sister had married his friend of the scheme. The west-country years of 1795-98 produced the conversation poems, the ballad volume and the two great unfinished romances, and a season at Göttingen in 1799-1800 brought him into contact with German philosophy and criticism. There followed public lectures on government and on the drama, the conduct of a weekly literary sheet at his own charge, a secretaryship in the British service at Malta, and a short government post that ended in quarrel with his patrons. From 1816 he lived in the north of England and then in London and its neighbourhood, at last in the house of a medical friend at Highgate, where he died in 1834. His long dependence on opium and laudanum, his estrangement from his family and his hopeless attachment to his wife's sister belong to the record of a nature of extraordinary intellectual appetite and imperfect execution.
literary_profile: His verse is small in bulk and central in influence: the supernatural ballad, the two unfinished romances, the vision of the pleasure-dome, and the conversation poems and odes of 1795-1802. His prose divides between critical and philosophical works, of which the literary autobiography is the chief, the essays of his weekly sheet, the treatise on the faculties of the mind, the sermons and charges on church and state, and the table-talk reported by friends and edited after his death. He is the originator of the Romantic distinction between fancy and imagination and of much of the vocabulary in which English criticism discusses symbol, organic form and belief.
stylistic_characteristics: In verse a command of several distinct mannerisms - the archaic reiteration of the ballad, the reiterated stress and internal music of the fragment, the soft suspended blank verse of the meditation and the exclamatory syntax of the ode; in prose a learned, abstract and often hortatory style, full of coined terms, of long definitions and of quotation from the moralists of the seventeenth century and of Germany.
intellectual_concerns: The imagination as a way of knowing and as the agent of all perception; the relation of philosophy to religion, and the distinction between reason and understanding; guilt, penance and the moral government of the universe; the education of the will, and the duties of the state and the clergy; the nature of poetic language and the faults of the substituted vocabulary of the eighteenth-century schools.
historical_significance: As poet he created the English supernatural ballad and the visionary fragment, and with the friend of the ballad volume he founded the Romantic poetry of imagination and of humble life; as critic and philosopher he transmitted the idealist philosophy to the nineteenth century and supplied the terms in which Romantic poetics has since been stated. His conversation, his printed lectures and his prose made him a governing presence in Victorian intellectual life, and his career remains the standard case of Romantic promise interrupted.
major_influences: The old English ballads and romances and the minstrely revival
the German philosophy and criticism read at Göttingen
the associationist psychology
the Platonising and mystical writers of the seventeenth century
the poetry of the friend of the ballad volume
the pre-Romantic ode and the blank-verse meditation
biographical_uncertainty: The date of composition of the vision of the pleasure-dome, and the chronology and extent of his opium use, are matters of continuing argument between biographers and textual scholars.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the confessional and analytical prose of the later Romantic period
literary_identity: Essayist, confessor and magazine writer, the most deliberate artist of prose rhythm among the Romantics and the first English writer to make the opium habit and the divided mind the sustained subject of a book.
biography: De Quincey was born at Manchester, the son of a merchant, and was educated at Manchester Grammar School, at boarding schools near London and at Bristol Grammar School. A rebellious adolescence took him away from his guardians and, by his own later account, into a period of wandering and destitution; he entered the University of Oxford in 1803 and left without a degree. Reading the poetry of the day led him to the Lake District, where in the years after 1808 he lived near the poets he admired, at one time in the cottage their family had quitted, and where he began the habit of opium that he described as governing his life. He settled in London as a contributor to the magazines, and his narrative of an opium eater, printed in a metropolitan periodical in 1821 and in book form the following year, made his name. From the middle of the decade he was a steady contributor to a leading Edinburgh magazine, publishing essays on literature, on German writing, on logic, on postage and on murder as a subject of taste, together with a long autobiographical sequel and a narrative of the mail-coach mail service. His later years were spent largely in Scotland, and he died at Edinburgh in December 1859, shortly after a fire at his lodgings had destroyed his papers and the stores of opium that had long been in his keeping.
literary_profile: His proper field is prose of a highly elaborated kind: the autobiographical confession and its sequel, the literary and political essay, the tale of murder and its parody of forensic reasoning, and a large body of periodical writing on books, on German literature and on the questions of the day. He published no volume of poetry and planned a vast history of literature and a learned dictionary that were never executed; his output was chiefly written for magazines and collected, often revised and often incompletely, after publication. His characteristic manner is the digressive essay that returns upon itself, with a passionate elaboration of the periodic sentence and a fondness for the nightmare image.
stylistic_characteristics: Prose built on long cadenced periods, balanced clauses, repeated keywords and sudden shifts from the ironic to the terrible, self-consciously modelled on the rhythms of Latin and English biblical prose; a irony that is carried by elaborate courtesy of tone; and a imagery of dreams, palaces, seas and pursuers that he himself discussed as the rhetoric of the opium vision.
intellectual_concerns: The divided and self-observing mind under stimulation; guilt, pursuit and the logic of crime as a pleasure of the intellect; literature as a power of expansion rather than of instruction; the machinery of the mind as studied by the metaphysicians; the social economy of letters and the condition of the magazine writer; the sublime and the pathetic as the two modes of great writing.
historical_significance: He created the modern literary confession of addiction and the literature of dream psychology, and his analytic tale of murder invented a form that the detective story later inherited; his essays on prose style, on the literature of knowledge and on the laws of rhetorical composition were among the most influential statements of the nineteenth century, and through them his work reaches the symbolists and the twentieth-century prose imaginations.
major_influences: The poetry and criticism of the Lake writers and of Coleridge
the German literature and romantic tale he read and reviewed in translation and in the original
the English prosaists of the seventeenth century and the Latin rhythmists
the political economy and the metaphysics of his own reading
the magazine and annual literary market of the 1820s and 1830s
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology and quantity of his opium use rest almost entirely on his own statements, which he allowed to be rhetorical; the dates and incidents of his wanderings in Wales as a boy, and of his first residence in the Lake District, cannot be verified independently and are differently reported in the biographies.

birthplace: London, in the Golden Square quarter, of a dissenting shopkeeping family
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, engraver and visionary painter of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Poet-engraver who made his books by his own hands, the creator of a private prophetic mythology, and the most uncompromising visionary writer of the English Romantic generation.
biography: Blake was born in London, the son of a hosier, and showed from early childhood a disposition to drawing and an familiarity with visions; he was not sent to school but was bound apprentice to an engraver at about fourteen, served the seven years, and then entered the schools of the Royal Academy, where the academic manner of the presidents offended him. He set up as an engraver and print-seller, married in 1782 a woman whom he taught to read and to work at his printing, and produced the illuminated books by a method of etching and relief-printing of his own invention, colouring the plates by hand and selling them in numbers far below their merit. He knew and was friendly with the painter of the Nightmare and with the publishers and dissenting writers of the revolutionary decade, visited France in 1792, and wrote and engraved the prophetic books of the years of hope and reaction. From 1800 to 1803 he worked under the patronage of a poet of the earlier school at Felpham in Sussex, where a soldier's complaint brought him before a magistrates' court and an acquittal; the last decades brought commissions for illustrations to a book of scripture and to the vision of the Italian poet, a small circle of devoted younger painters, a display of his own designs at his own price, and death in 1827 in lodging in the Strand, his wife beside him and his funeral attended by friends of both his arts.
literary_profile: His writing divides between the songs and shorter lyrics of the two illuminated collections, the prophetic books in verse and prose, and the mass of annotations, memoranda, letters and designs; his mythology of the four powers of the human mind, of the fallen reason and of the labouring imagination is the most systematic private system in English. He was also a designer and engraver whose plates carry his poems, so that text and image must be read as one, and a painter in water-colour and in tempera who executed a series of large designs and illustrations.
stylistic_characteristics: Lyric verse of great simplicity in song measures, with reiterated lines and a balance of innocent and terrible images; prophetic verse of stern and rapid accentual lines, filled with proclamation, question and catalogue; prose of aphoristic vehemence, with the rhetoric of the angel and the devil and a continuous war of contraries.
intellectual_concerns: The contraries by which the soul progresses, and the falseness of a morality of patience and restraint; imagination as the divine body in man and the enemy of single reason; the guilt of law, priesthood and empire, and the bondage of the slave, the child and the inhibited lover; the redemption of the divided giant and the building of a city of vision in England.
historical_significance: He anticipated by a decade the ballad revolt against polished verse, and he left the only fully developed personal mythology in English. His illuminated books are the foundation of the art of the printed page in which poem and design are one object, and his prophecy of a redeemed imagination, with his phrases for the dark satanic mills and for the child and the sweep, has entered the language of literature, of religious radicalism and of national song.
major_influences: The dissenting and enthusiast traditions of the English Civil War century
the mystical and theological writers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries
the engraver's study of the older Italian and northern designs
the revolutionary writing of the 1790s
the religious systems of the radicals then in fashion
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of the first issue of several illuminated books and the order in which the plates were executed and sold are disputed, and the account of his visions rests almost wholly on his own statements and on those of his wife and his friends.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Radical criticism and the periodical essay of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Critic, essayist and polemicist, the leading English reviewer of his generation and the most forceful writer of character-sketches in prose, who also held an office in the Excise and tried for a while to earn his living as a painter.
biography: Hazlitt was born at Maidstone, the son of a Unitarian minister who took the family to America during the Revolutionary war and returned to England in the middle of the 1780s. He was educated for his father's profession at the Warrington Academy, where the new philosophical theology was taught, and for a short time afterwards attended lectures in Scotland; he never took holy orders. He tried painting, working as a portrait painter and as an engraver of portraits, and he held a salaried post in the Excise, which for years made his literary work possible. From about 1813 he wrote theatrical and political criticism for the liberal journals of the day, most importantly for Leigh Hunt's Examiner, and he contributed essays and reviews to other periodicals until his death. He lectured on poetry and on the drama in London in 1818, 1819 and 1820, and his published lectures, his characters of the dramatists and his series of contemporary portraits made him the most discussed critic of the period. A long attachment, exposed in a printed confession in 1822, coincided with the breach of his marriage and with years of quarrel, debt and ill health; his books were sold to meet his obligations, and he died in Frith Street, Soho, in September 1830, in the poor circumstances his own essays had often described.
literary_profile: His work divides between criticism, philosophical writing and the essay. He edited and annotated the English poets, wrote continuously on the stage, and practised in his magazines and lectures the character-writing that he defined as the critic's proper task; his earliest and most ambitious book was a treatise on the human mind in its action, which he long considered the foundation of all his other work. His prose subjects are the theatre and the poets, the painting of Italy, the political conflict of his own decade, and the temper of the ages he read. He is at his strongest in the short analytical sketch, where a single quality of a writer or a public figure is followed out to its consequences.
stylistic_characteristics: An assertive, colloquial and heavily accented prose, built on balance, contrast and blunt verdict, with a sustained rhetorical momentum in the paragraphs of the essays; a habit of opening with a general proposition and closing with a personal one; imagery drawn from painting, from the theatre and from the landscape, and an unapologetic first person that turns criticism into a form of autobiography.
intellectual_concerns: The association of ideas as the ground of mind and of taste; liberty of thought and the hatred of tyranny, in politics as in the theatre; the distinction between power and genius; imagination as the faculty that enlarges sympathy; the prejudice and self-interest of the established orders; the relation of the age to its writers.
historical_significance: He is the principal English critic between Johnson and the Victorians, and his method of describing the dominant faculty of a writer set the pattern for later character-writing; his Shakespearean and Jacobean criticism, his account of the poets of his own age, and his essays on the principles of the mind together form the most complete body of Romantic critical prose outside German idealism, and his political writing is a primary record of English Radicalism in the years of repression.
major_influences: The Unitarian intellectual culture of Warrington and its teachers
the philosophical writings of the eighteenth century on association and on the passions
Rousseau and the French writers of the Revolution
the English poets and dramatists of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries
the painting of Italy seen at first hand
the example and friendship of the liberal journals of his own decade
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of his student years in Scotland and of his first contributions to the periodicals are not exactly settled, and the chronology and the details of the attachment described in the printed confession of 1822 are known chiefly from his own account, which is a literary representation rather than a record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Lake school of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Poet and theorist of poetry of the Lake District, the maker of the lyrical ballad and of the Romantic blank-verse meditation, and the most authoritative English voice on nature, memory and the growing mind.
biography: Wordsworth was born at Cockermouth in Cumberland, the second of five children of an estate agent, and was educated at Hawkshead grammar school and at St John's College, Cambridge. He walked the mountains in his student holidays, and stayed in France in 1790 and again in 1791-95, when the early promise of the Revolution made a lasting impression on him and a daughter, Caroline, was born there. Settling with his sister Dorothy first at Racedown and then at Alfoxden in the west, he began in 1797-98 the collaboration that produced the anonymous ballad volume; in 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson, and after the Keswick years he settled at Allan Bank and then at Rydal Mount, where he lived until his death. The later decades brought public employment as Distributor of Stamps for Westmorland, an unfinished scheme of a philosophical poem, the volumes of 1807, The Excursion of 1814, the Ecclesiastical Sketches of 1822, and a national fame marked by a civil pension and by the laureateship accepted in 1843. The autobiographical poem on the growth of a poet's mind, long revised and never published by its author, appeared after his death in 1850. His politics moved from revolutionary sympathy to a conservative attachment to church, state and the rural order, a change much used against him by later critics.
literary_profile: His work divides between the lyrical ballads and short lyrics of humble life, the blank-verse meditations and sonnets, and the long philosophical and autobiographical poem planned as The Recluse, of which only The Excursion was published in his lifetime. He wrote also a prose guide to his own country and a large body of letters and memoranda, and his Preface to Lyrical Ballads is the period's most quoted theory of poetry. His subjects are the mountain landscape, the labouring poor, children, grief and endurance, and the education of the imagination, and his characteristic form is the poem that passes from an observed scene to a history of the mind that remembers it.
stylistic_characteristics: A deliberate plainness of diction drawn from ordinary speech, rising in the blank verse to great weight of syntax; long suspensive periods, apostrophe, repetition and an insistent use of general nouns; in the lyrics a song-like regularity of stanza and refrain, and in the sonnets a compressed and Latinate turn. The manner changes markedly between the deliberate roughness of the experimental ballads and the serenity of the later lyrics.
intellectual_concerns: The mind's intercourse with nature and the shaping power of landscape; memory and the pleasure re-created in tranquillity; the imagination as a moral and perceptual faculty; childhood as the season of vision; the loss of revolutionary hope and its consolation in duty, the church and the permanences of rural life; the proper language and audience of poetry.
historical_significance: With the collaborators of the ballad volume he opened the English Romantic period and supplied its most durable account of how poems are made; his blank-verse meditation and his autobiographical poem founded the modern poetry of the self's education, and his sonnets helped revive the English sonnet. His practice and his theory together changed the subject and the diction of English verse, and his later career remains the central case in the long argument about the relation between Romantic poetry and political allegiance.
major_influences: The mountain landscape of the north-west and the walking tours of his youth
the French Revolution and its disappointment
the ballad and minstrely revival of the 1790s
Milton and the blank-verse tradition
the eighteenth-century topographical and descriptive poets
the associationist psychology of his reading
his sister Dorothy and the friendship and disagreement of the ballad volume's collaborator
biographical_uncertainty: The sequence of his French sojourns of the early 1790s and the circumstances of his daughter Caroline's parentage and upbringing are recorded imperfectly and are variously stated in the biographies.
